title: Minimum Increment to Make Array Unique
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> count: size maxVal + n + 1 ≤ 2·10^5 + 1 → O(n + V)
- no recursion, no heap, no other containers
- not counted: input nums
approach: Use a frequency (counting) array indexed by value. Process values from smallest to largest: whenever a value v has more than one occurrence, the extra copies each need at least one increment to move to v+1, so we add the extra count to the move total and push those extras into count[v+1]. This cascade continues naturally, and because we always push duplicates to the very next slot, every increment is necessary and sufficient - no element is moved further than it must be. The count array is sized maxVal + n + 1 to accommodate the worst-case cascade where all n duplicates push past the original maximum.
hints:
When two elements share the same value, where must the "extra" copies eventually land relative to that value?
Each move increments exactly one element by 1, and nums[i] ranges from 0 to 10^5.

Use a frequency array indexed by value. For [3,2,1,2,1,7], value 1 appears twice: push one copy to value 2 (cost 1), making value 2 appear three times total, then push two copies to value 3 (cost 2), and so on cascading upward.

```
count = frequency array of size maxVal + n + 1
for v from 0 to size - 2:
    if count[v] > 1:
        extra = count[v] - 1
        moves += extra
        count[v + 1] += extra
return moves
```

**Single element** - no duplicates exist
`Input: [5]` → `Expected: 0`
⚠️ Bug: initializing moves to 1 instead of 0 → returns 1

**All equal** - every element is the same value
`Input: [1,1,1]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: count array sized maxVal+1 (=2), count[2] and count[3] accessed out of bounds → crash

**All zeros** - minimum value boundary
`Input: [0,0,0,0]` → `Expected: 6`
⚠️ Bug: loop starting at v=1 instead of v=0 → skips count[0] entirely, returns 0

**Cascade beyond maxVal** - duplicates push past the largest original value
`Input: [3,3,3,3]` → `Expected: 6`
⚠️ Bug: count array sized maxVal+1 (=4), count[4..6] accessed out of bounds → crash

followUps.q: What if nums[i] can be up to 10^9 instead of 10^5?
followUps.a: The frequency array becomes too large. Sort the array, then greedily process in sorted order: for each element, if it is ≤ the last assigned value, set it to last+1 and add the difference to moves. This gives O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space with an in-place sort.

followUps.q: What if you must also return the final unique array, not just the move count?
followUps.a: After the counting pass determines how many copies land at each value, do a second pass over the original array: for each element, assign it to the smallest unused value ≥ its original value, tracked via the residual count array. Time and space complexity remain O(n + V).

followUps.q: What if the array arrives as a stream of unknown length and you must output the running total after each element?
followUps.a: Maintain the frequency array and a pointer to the current "frontier" value. When a new element arrives, increment its count; if that creates a duplicate, cascade from that value upward exactly as before, adding to the running total. Each insertion triggers at most O(V) cascade work amortized, giving O(n + V) total time and O(V) space.
